19.0.s.en: (1) Hezekiah asks for the prayer of Isaiah, who reassures him

19.0.0.en: When Hezekiah heard Sennacherib's blasphemies against God, he was deeply grieved and tore his clothes, like his three officials, as the last verse of the previous chapter mentions. Hezekiah put on sackcloth, as a sign of his humility, and went to the house of the Lord to cry out to Him, that He might deliver him and defend His holy name. Hezekiah shows how the children of God act in distress before their enemies. When someone threatens the kings of the world with war, they gather their counselors and the commanders of their armies to answer their enemies; Hezekiah, however, took refuge in God before anything else.

19.1.0.en: Hezekiah sent Eliakim, the master of the palace, and Shebna the scribe, together with the senior priests, clothed in sackcloth, to the prophet Isaiah, carrying a message to him from the king. All were grieved at the blasphemy against the name of God. We notice Hezekiah's recourse to Isaiah, the prophet of God: he goes to the house of the Lord and to His prophet, which means that his trust in God is complete, and his reliance upon Him.

19.1.1.en: We see Hezekiah's concern in sending those who had heard the Assyrian blasphemies, and in sending with them his greatest assistants; he takes refuge in God with all his strength. The king's envoys came to Isaiah and told him Hezekiah's message.

19.1.2.en: When difficult problems and threats confront you, take refuge in God first, however bewildering the matter may be. Pray, and seek the guidance of your father of confession, and you will hear the voice of God, and He will guide you in everything.

19.2.0.en: Hezekiah declared through his envoys, who were sent to Isaiah, that the distress they were passing through was very severe, because Sennacherib was stronger than they, and he threatens and blasphemes the name of God, while they are weaker than Sennacherib and cannot answer him; but all their hope is in God, who is able to answer him sharply. He likens the condition of the people to women with child whose time of delivery has come, yet they have no strength for it. They are the people of God, and their God is mighty, able to bring forth the fruit from the womb, that is, to defend His people; and though it has not yet happened, they are waiting for God to intervene.

19.3.0.en: "It may be that the Lord your God will hear what the Rabshakeh has said, whom his master the king of Assyria sent to reproach the living God, and will rebuke him for the words that he has spoken; so pray for the remnant that survives among us," after the kingdom of Israel was taken captive (ch. 18:10, 11). Nothing was left to Hezekiah but the city of Jerusalem and those in it. So he declares his weakness and his humility before God, that He may have mercy on him and deliver him from the hand of Sennacherib. And certainly God will not forsake the one who takes refuge in Him with faith and humility.

19.4.0.en: Isaiah reassured Hezekiah's envoys and gave them a message for their king, that he should not be afraid of the servants of the king of Assyria, whom he calls lads, perhaps as a belittling of them and of their power, which is nothing before God. He foretold to them that Sennacherib would hear a rumor that would make him want to return to his own land. This rumor was the advance of Tirhakah king of Ethiopia, his seizing of Egypt, and then his preparing to attack Assyria.

19.5.s.en: (2) The king of Assyria continues his threats

19.5.0.en: Libnah: a city in southern Judah, between Makkedah and Lachish.

19.5.1.en: The Rabshakeh, the official spokesman for Sennacherib, left the Assyrian army besieging Jerusalem and returned to his king at Lachish, and found that he had left it and gone to fight against Libnah, perhaps hoping that by seizing the city of Libnah, which belonged to Judah, he would weaken Jerusalem and frighten them, so that it would surrender to him.

19.6.0.en: The king of Assyria was told that Tirhakah king of Cush had declared war on him, so he felt the need to seize Jerusalem, in order to strengthen his position against Tirhakah and be free to fight him. He therefore sent to Hezekiah to threaten him and frighten him a second time, since Hezekiah's weakness had appeared before, when he paid silver and gold and declared his submission (ch. 18:14).

19.7.0.en: Although Sennacherib was in extreme fear of Tirhakah, he pretended to be strong and sent to threaten Hezekiah and to make him doubt the power of his God, as though He were unable to protect him from the king of Assyria.

19.8.0.en: Gozan: it lies on the river Habor, north of Babylon, in the Assyrian kingdom.

19.8.1.en: Haran: it lies near the river Euphrates, on a trade route; caravans came to it from Damascus, Nineveh and Carchemish.

19.8.2.en: Rezeph: a city located in present-day Iraq, between Hamath and the Euphrates.

19.8.3.en: The children of Eden: they lived near the river Euphrates, and their capital was Telassar, which means the hill of Assyria.

19.8.4.en: Arpad, the city of Sepharvaim, Hena and Ivah: see (ch. 17:24, 18:34). The Rabshakeh continued his threats to Hezekiah, reminding him of what the kings of Assyria had done to the peoples who tried to rebel against Assyria, and how they triumphed over them, and the gods of those nations were not able to defend them. Of course, your God will not be able to deliver you, for He is like these gods, powerless before the might of the kings of Assyria.

19.8.5.en: "Many there be which say of my soul, There is no help for him in God" (Ps 3:2). Beloved, the war is one, though the time differs: it is casting doubt on the power of God and the right hand of His might, so that you lose your faith and your hope... Do not be anxious, but be strengthened; and if the wars weigh heavily upon you, flee to the bosom of your father of confession and the embrace of your Church... there you will find help.

19.9.0.en: Hezekiah received the letters of threat from the hands of the messengers of the king of Assyria who had brought them to him, and after he had read their contents he went into the temple and spread them before the Lord.

19.9.1.en: We notice that the Assyrian threats this time were written, to frighten the children of Israel, but Hezekiah entered the house of the Lord in faith, asking Him to defend His name against the mockery of the nations. He was confident of the power of God, which would work and be glorified.

19.10.0.en: Hezekiah prayed before the Lord, saying: O Lord God of Israel, who sit enthroned, borne by the angels, You are the only God of all the peoples of the earth. You made heaven and earth. In this he declared that God alone is God, above the angels and the Creator of the whole world.

19.11.0.en: Incline Your ear, O Lord, to the blasphemies of the king of Assyria, and look upon the words of Sennacherib, which he sent to me to reproach You, O God; You alone are the living God.

19.12.0.en: It is true, O Lord, what the kings of Assyria have done, laying waste the lands and countries of those peoples and burning their gods, which did not resist, because they are idols and false gods, but the work of men's hands, of wood and stone.

19.13.0.en: Hezekiah implored the Lord, saying: Deliver us, O Lord, from the hand of the king of Assyria, that all the kingdoms of the earth may know that You alone are the true God. Hezekiah's confidence in God appears in his asking Him to intervene now, that is, quickly, so that His name may be glorified. He is jealous for the name of God and trusts in His power. Out of his love, Hezekiah cannot bear that the name of God be insulted in his presence, and he wants God to show His power, that perhaps the peoples may believe and submit to Him.

19.13.1.en: Speak with confidence to God in prayer, especially when some mock His power or speak ill of Him, and ask Him to reveal His glory, to support you and to deliver you from all who surround you. For He is above all and able to do all things.

19.14.0.en: The Lord's answer to the prayer of Hezekiah was swift, for He sent to him through the prophet Isaiah, saying: The Lord has heard what you complained to Him about concerning Sennacherib king of Assyria. This means God's care, and that He will act and protect him and punish those who exalt themselves against him.

19.15.0.en: Has shaken: shook her head in mockery at the one before her.

19.15.1.en: God's answer to Hezekiah's prayer was spoken through Isaiah as he addresses Sennacherib. He speaks of the people of God, likening it to a virgin and a maiden: it appears with the weakness of a virgin and a maiden, but its strength is mighty in its God who supports it. This virgin has despised you, Sennacherib, and mocked you. He says this in the past tense because God has decided to take vengeance on Sennacherib and his army, who mocked God; and since God has decided, what He has commanded will surely come to pass, so He spoke in the past tense. For God had used Assyria to discipline His people, that they might repent, but He loves His people very much, so when they cried out to Him with humility, repentance and faith, He hastened to help them and to take vengeance on Assyria, who became proud and thought that its strength was from itself, and did not understand that this was by a temporary permission from God, to discipline the people of God.

19.16.0.en: God continues His rebuke of Sennacherib, saying to him: How did you dare to mock and blaspheme the Holy One, the God of the children of Israel? Of course these words reached the Assyrian army through some people coming out of Jerusalem, or God declared them through one of the men of Jerusalem from the wall, and the Assyrian army heard them.

19.17.0.en: Ascent: a road on the top of the heights.

19.17.1.en: The cedar: a great, hard, tall, evergreen tree, abundant on the mountains of Lebanon.

19.17.2.en: The cypress: a kind of tall coniferous tree, cone-shaped.

19.17.3.en: Rugged: a road that is not smoothed, with rocks and stones; but what is meant here is forests that cannot be penetrated because of the density of their trees.

19.17.4.en: Carmel: a range of mountains covered with dense trees in Lebanon.

19.17.5.en: God continues and exposes the pride of Sennacherib's arrogant and haughty heart, which exalted itself against the very name of God and against His messengers, that is, Hezekiah's envoys, and boasted that he had invaded all the high countries and the dense forests with their lofty trees, and that no chief or difficult road stood before his chariots, for he cut through and removed every obstacle. Sennacherib wrote these words in his letter to Hezekiah, and God now reveals them to show the extent of his pride.

19.18.0.en: After Sennacherib proudly declared in the previous verse his dominion over the kings and rulers of the nations, here, in this verse, he declares his authority over all the peoples of the earth. He says proudly, "I." His drinking strange waters means that he had seized many countries foreign to him, and taken their goods and drunk their waters. Also Egypt, the empire that preceded him and still a strong state: he declares that he entered it with his very great armies and drank its waters until there was no water left in it, and trampled its rivers with the soles of his soldiers' feet, declaring his dominion, his strength and his enormous hosts. These words, too, Sennacherib did not write or declare, as we mentioned in the previous verse.

19.19.0.en: Hills: plural of hill, which is elevated ground.

19.19.1.en: Sennacherib said proudly before to Hezekiah in (v. 11), Have you not heard of the power of the kings of Assyria, which shattered all the surrounding peoples? Now God answers the king of Assyria and says to him: Have you not heard what I have done? From of old, that is, from eternity, I planned in My design to make you, Sennacherib, an instrument for shattering peoples. You are merely an instrument in My hand, but you exalted yourself against Me and thought yourself something when many nations submitted to you. And God asks the king of Assyria: Have you not heard of My power in the prophecies of My prophets and My work with My people? How then did you dare to stand before Me and be proud against Me? I divided the Red Sea and indeed dried up the ground in the days of Moses, and likewise in the days of Joshua I stopped the waters in the river Jordan, but you speak of delusions and did not truly dry up the sea.

19.20.0.en: Blasted: plants that dried up and were burned by the hot wind that blew upon them.

19.20.1.en: God describes the inhabitants of the countries that the king of Assyria invaded as weak, likening them to people with short hands, unable to defend themselves, because they depend on idols and not on God. He likens them also, when Assyria attacked them and they were afraid and pierced, to weak grass that grows in the fields, and to tender, weak green plants in the beginning of their growth, before they have strong stalks and fruit. He likens them also to the grass on the housetops, which is weak and short because it has no depth; and finally he likens them to small plants whose growth was not complete, upon which hot winds blew, drying them and burning them.

19.21.0.en: God addresses the king of Assyria, saying that He sees everything: He sees all his movements, his deeds, his words, his pride and his exalting himself against God. God is longsuffering, hoping that he may repent, but of course He will punish him as long as he persists in this pride.

19.22.0.en: Hook: a metal ring put in the nose of slaves to humiliate them.

19.22.1.en: Bridle: a piece of iron put in the mouth of a horse to lead it as its rider wishes.

19.22.2.en: God said to Sennacherib: I have heard your pride and your rage against Me, I who dwell on high, and this pride has come up to Me; and of course I will punish you, as you punished many kings when you seized them and put hooks in their noses. This idea had been devised by the kings of the Assyrians to humiliate those whom they conquered, so now God does it to them, or speaks to them with it, and they understand it; that is, God will humble the king of Assyria like a lowly slave, then master him as the rider masters the horse, and bring him back to his country fleeing before the power of God, as we shall see at the end of this chapter.

19.22.3.en: Do not be proud toward those around you, for you are being proud toward God; and if, in His longsuffering, He gives you opportunities for repentance, do not waste them, lest He punish you and you be brought down to the ground in lowliness and humiliation.

19.23.0.en: Aftergrowth: fruit gathered from the same plant that was sown in the land in the previous year. After the harvest is gathered in the first year, the stalks of the plants are left in the ground and give fruit in the following year; this is called aftergrowth.

19.23.1.en: That which springs of the same: grains that fall during the harvest and give plants and fruit as aftergrowth.

19.23.2.en: Then God gave Hezekiah signs to reassure him that He was with him and would not forsake him. After Hezekiah is rid of the Assyrians by the power of God, God also takes care to feed His people, so He permits seed to fall while the Assyrians gather the harvests of the Jews, and this seed grows into plants and gives a harvest sufficient for all the Jews remaining in the kingdom of Judah in this year. Then in the following year He makes the same plants bear fruit, sufficient also for His people in the following year, because the following year was a seventh year, in which the Law forbids cultivating the land and it is left to rest; so God, without any sowing, will make the same plants give aftergrowth for His people to eat. It is known in agriculture that the aftergrowth is less and weaker than in the first year, but by the blessing of God He makes the harvest abundant and sufficient for His people. In the third year, they begin to cultivate the land, because they will be secure in God's protection, having restored the fortification and renewal of their cities.

19.23.3.en: In this we see that God feels for His people, whom the Assyrians wronged, eating their food, so He gives them instead food sufficient for them that they did not sow: the self-sown grain, and then in the second year the aftergrowth.

19.23.4.en: This prophecy signifies God's blessing upon His people: although Assyria persecuted it and killed many, God blesses the remnant, so that they multiply and become a great nation.

19.23.5.en: Do not fear the trials that come upon you, or the wrong done to you by others, for God is able to compensate you many times over for all that you have lost. Be reassured, for you are under the protection of your God, who is able to do all things.

19.24.0.en: God promises His people that after the defeat of the wicked and their flight, the people who escaped destruction will return, and because of the blessings of their God they will become like strong, tall trees with spreading roots and will produce various fruits, as a sign of the revival of the people after the distress. Not only this, but the jealousy of the mighty Lord, the God of hosts, for His name and for His people (His bride) makes Him scatter His enemies and crush everyone who exalted himself against His bride. It can also be said that it is a prophecy about the Church: however weak it may seem at some times, persecuted and lacking strength, its heavenly Bridegroom will defend it, and the gates of Hades shall not prevail against it.

19.24.1.en: Do not despair at the multitude of trials and the weakness that appears in you, and the multitude of your falls, and even the reproaches of the wicked, for all of them are temporary and will end, as long as you have taken refuge in God in repentance and contrition. He will compensate you for all that you have missed, and you will live with Him in strength and bear much spiritual fruit.

19.25.0.en: Shield: a piece of wood covered with leather, with a handle at the back into which the soldier puts his hand and moves it in front of his head and body to defend himself.

19.25.1.en: Siege mound (bank): a wall built by the enemy to take cover behind it and hurl stones or fire from behind it, and to prevent those leaving the besieged city from escaping.

19.25.2.en: Despite the strength of the Assyrian siege of Jerusalem, God reassures Hezekiah that the enemy will not be able to enter Jerusalem and use his weapons against it, but will return to his own country.

19.26.0.en: God affirms that He will protect His city Jerusalem for the glorifying of His holy name, which the enemies reproached. The second reason for protecting His city is His honoring of David, great in his godliness, from whose seed comes King Hezekiah who sits on his throne.

19.26.1.en: God honors His saints and answers their intercession; therefore we take refuge in them and ask for their mediation.

19.27.s.en: (5) The destruction of Sennacherib and his army

19.27.0.en: It happened that night that the angel of the Lord came to the camp of the Assyrians and destroyed a hundred and eighty-five thousand of their soldiers. And when day broke, their corpses filled the camp. We notice that God's punishment was very swift: on the night of the very day on which God announced His punishment, He carried out the sentence on Sennacherib and his army, because their pride was great.

19.28.0.en: Sennacherib was able to escape with a small number of his army, and he hurried to Nineveh, his capital.

19.28.1.en: Perhaps in this he thought that he had escaped the divine punishment, but a punishment awaited him that we cannot imagine, which we shall see in the next verse.

19.29.0.en: Ararat: a plateau lying east of present-day Iraq, on which Noah's ark came to rest.

19.29.1.en: Sennacherib was in deep despair when he returned to Nineveh, so he took refuge in his god Nisroch in his temple, that he might support him, and bowed down before the idol. There God carried out His judgment, in a way Sennacherib did not expect, for his two sons attacked him and killed him with the sword, then fled to the plateau of Ararat.

19.29.2.en: Then another son of his, called Esarhaddon, reigned after him.

19.29.3.en: We notice that Hezekiah passed through three stages in his relationship with God in the face of the Assyrian attack:

19.29.4.en: 1- He relied on himself, so he was afraid and sought a human solution; he declared his submission and servitude to the king of Assyria and sent him silver and gold (ch. 18:14-16).

19.29.5.en: 2- When Sennacherib deceived him and attacked him and seized the cities of Judah and besieged Jerusalem, Hezekiah found nothing before him but to take refuge in God, that He might deliver him (v. 1).

19.29.6.en: 3- When Sennacherib reproached the name of God and blasphemed it, Hezekiah asked God to intervene and defend His name, for he was attached to the love of God and jealous for His holy name (v. 16). In the beginning he relied on himself; the second time he felt his weakness and that of his people and his great need of God; but the third time his heart was attached to God and jealous for His holy name. So the distress made Hezekiah grow in his relationship with God.

19.29.7.en: The power of God is able to do all things and works beyond what a man thinks. Therefore do not be troubled, however great the power of your enemies who wrong you, for God is able to deliver you from their hands, in a way you do not expect.

19.29.8.en: The lengthening of Hezekiah's life, then his pride
